stem: A sexually active adult asks how to reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Which nursing teaching best reflects current CDC prevention guidance?

options.A: Use condoms correctly every time, discuss STI testing and results with partners and the health care provider, and receive indicated vaccines such as HPV or hepatitis B when eligible.
options.B: If a partner looks healthy and has no symptoms, STI testing and safer-sex practices are unnecessary.
options.C: Condoms eliminate the risk of every STI, including infections transmitted through uncovered skin-to-skin contact.
options.D: STI prevention is relevant only after symptoms appear because asymptomatic infections cannot be transmitted.

rationale: CDC prevention guidance recommends safer-sex strategies such as correct condom use, appropriate STI testing, communication with partners and health care providers, and vaccination for preventable infections such as HPV and hepatitis B when indicated. Many STIs can be asymptomatic, so lack of symptoms does not establish that a person is uninfected. Condoms reduce risk but do not provide absolute protection against all infections, especially those spread by skin-to-skin contact.
educational_objective: Teach evidence-based STI risk-reduction strategies and correct misconceptions about asymptomatic infection and the limits of condom protection.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: How to Prevent STIs; Getting Tested for STIs; Individuals — Talk. Test. Treat.
source_version_date: Prevention page April 9, 2024; testing and communication pages March 17, 2026
source_locator: How to Prevent STIs > Prevention steps and strategies: vaccination, fewer partners, regular testing, mutually monogamous tested partner, condoms used correctly every time. Getting Tested: STIs often have no symptoms and testing depends on risk. Talk.Test.Treat.: open partner/provider communication and correct condom use.
source_claim_supported: CDC recommends a combination of safer-sex practices, risk-appropriate testing, partner/provider communication, and indicated vaccination; asymptomatic infection is possible and condoms reduce but do not eliminate all STI risk.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance, printed p.9/PDF p.13: Provide education about prevention, screening, immunization, and health practices
blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — STI prevention education
correction_summary: Retained the prevention construct but replaced the vague bundled phrase 'barrier use, screening, communication, vaccination' with CDC-specific teaching: correct condom use, risk-appropriate testing, partner/provider communication, and indicated vaccination. Added the current CDC caveats that STIs may be asymptomatic and condoms do not eliminate all skin-to-skin transmission risk.

audit_findings.source_authority: PASS — CDC is the primary U.S. public-health authority for STI prevention guidance.
audit_findings.currentness: PASS — current CDC testing/communication material updated March 17, 2026 and prevention page rechecked 2026-08-17.
audit_findings.exact_locator: PASS — cited sections directly support every element of the correct answer and the distractor exclusions.
audit_findings.stem: PASS — broad adult prevention counseling without assuming a specific risk profile that would change testing intervals.
audit_findings.correct_answer: PASS — A accurately states generally applicable CDC prevention strategies while using 'indicated' for vaccines.
audit_findings.distractors: PASS — B and D conflict with asymptomatic transmission/testing guidance; C overstates condom protection.
audit_findings.rationale: PASS — avoids claiming universal screening intervals or complete condom protection.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: PASS — only A is consistent with all cited CDC guidance.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — options are counseling statements with comparable form.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — prevention, screening education, and immunization align with Health Promotion and Maintenance.
